title: Ekpang Nkukwo with Water Yam
author: Chinelo Okafor
desc: Four pounds of cocoyam and water yam together, wrapped a tablespoon at a time, with one and a half to two cups of palm oil — forty-five minutes on medium heat.
longDesc: This is the richer, larger version. Four pounds of cocoyam and water yam go in together — the water yam is this recipe's own addition and it makes the paste stickier and easier to wrap — and the wraps are a tablespoon each rather than a teaspoon. The palm oil is dramatically more generous at a cup and a half to two cups, which gives a deeply red, oily pot rather than a lightly coloured one. Three cups of shelled periwinkle and a tablespoon of ground country onions are the other markers. The whole thing takes forty-five minutes on medium heat.
ingredients: 1 1/2 - 2 cups palm oil or red oil
steps: Shred the cocoyam and water yam, or pulse them with a blender to give that grated feel. Add a little salt and leave until ready to use.
Tear the cocoyam leaves into usable pieces.
Put one tablespoon of the grated mixture onto a torn leaf and wrap it up firmly, so the cocoyam is not coming out at all.
Layer the wraps into the pot.
Make a stock with the boiled beef, dried fish, crayfish, onion, seasoning, country onions, white pepper and scotch bonnet, and cook it 10 minutes.
Pour the stock over the wraps and add the periwinkle.
Cook 45 minutes on medium heat, shaking rather than stirring.
Add the palm oil partway through, lifting gently so it distributes.
Finish with the bitter leaf and serve.
chefTips: Wrap firmly, so the cocoyam is not coming out at all. A loose wrap disintegrates and thickens the pot instead of staying a parcel.
Water yam alongside the cocoyam makes the paste stickier and markedly easier to wrap. That is this version's own addition.
A tablespoon per wrap here, against a teaspoon in the other documented version. Larger parcels, longer cooking — forty-five minutes rather than about twenty before the first shake.
One and a half to two cups of palm oil is an enormous amount relative to the other version's two cooking spoons. It gives a very different, much richer dish. Start lower if you are unsure.
Country onions — not onions at all, but a West African spice seed. A tablespoon, ground.
Tear the leaves rather than cutting them. Torn edges wrap more willingly.
Shake, never stir, exactly as in the other version. That instruction is consistent across both sources.
commonMistakes: Wrapping loosely so the parcels burst.
Using only cocoyam, which makes a drier paste that is harder to wrap.
Adding all the palm oil at the start.
Cutting the leaves with a knife.
servedWith: On its own, as a one-pot
sources: Adapted from 'Ekpang Nkukwo: An Efik and Ibibio delicacy', byline Chinelo Eze, Guardian Nigeria, 9 March 2022. Quantities as printed: 4 pounds cocoyam and water yam; 3 cups shelled periwinkle (optional); 4-5 bunch cocoyam leafy greens; 1/2 pound boiled beef; 1-2 cups dried fish; 1/2 cup ground crayfish; 1/2 medium onion chopped; 1 1/2-2 cups palm oil/red oil; seasoning cubes; 1 tbsp ground country onions; 1 tbsp white pepper; 1 scotch bonnet pepper; 1 tbsp bitter leaf; salt and pepper to taste. Stock 10 minutes; total cooking 45 minutes on medium heat. Yield not specified.
Headnote places the dish with the Efik and Ibibio peoples of eastern Nigeria, and also with the Bakweri of Cameroon.
THE WRAPPING, as printed: one tablespoon of grated cocoyam on a torn leaf, 'wrap up firmly that the cocoyam is not coming out at all.'

DISAGREEMENT ON PORTION SIZE, not reconciled: a tablespoon here against a teaspoon-size in the 1Q Food Platter version (NGA071) — a threefold difference, from two sources that otherwise describe the same dish.

MAJOR DISAGREEMENT ON PALM OIL, not reconciled: 1 1/2 to 2 cups here against 2 cooking spoons there. That is roughly an order of magnitude and it produces a genuinely different dish. Both are published.
FURTHER DIFFERENCE: this version uses 4 pounds of cocoyam AND water yam together; the other uses 6 medium cocoyam and no water yam at all.

THE GRATING ENDPOINT, confirmed absent here too: 'Shred the cocoyam or pulse with a blender to give that grated feel. When done, add a little salt and leave till ready to use.' 'That grated feel' defines the endpoint by the word being defined, which is not a cue. Two sources, neither with one.

A FINDING WORTH RECORDING ABOUT SOURCES GENERALLY: newspapers did not quantify better than blogs in this research. Guardian Nigeria gave full quantities here; Vanguard gave none for fisherman's soup (NGA074) or for ikokore; GbaramatuVoice gave full quantities for kekefiyai (NGA075) and none for onunu (NGA076). Institutional provenance did not predict rigour.
reheating: Low heat with a splash of water, no stirring.
healthBenefits: Cocoyam and water yam are both high in potassium and resistant starch.
Three cups of periwinkle makes this exceptionally high in iron.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
culturalNote: The two documented ekpang nkukwo recipes differ so sharply on palm oil — two cooking spoons against two cups — that they are effectively two dishes under one name. One is a light cocoyam parcel stew; the other is a deep red, oil-rich pot. Both come from named sources writing about the same Efik and Ibibio tradition, and the gap between them is a fair measure of how much range a Nigerian dish name can cover.
